summary: Use fewer, memorable songs (such as one main theme with arrangements), let realistic visuals be backed by realistic ambient sound instead of music that sticks out, and make every song fit what the player is feeling.
takeaways: Use fewer songs more effectively; huge soundtracks are hard to remember
Build arrangements of one main theme throughout the game
Realistic graphics call for realistic ambient sounds, balanced in the mix
Make songs complement how the player is feeling

principles.principle: Build the soundtrack on a main theme and its arrangements
principles.why: Huge soundtracks are harder to remember or get excited by, and a song has more impact when people can remember its melody.
principles.how: Write one main theme, then reuse arrangements of it across the game instead of producing many unrelated songs.
principles.anti_pattern: Producing too many songs for a single game.
principles.quote: However you do it, a song will have more impact if people can remember its melody.

principles.principle: Back realistic visuals with realistic ambient sound, each layer given proper presence
principles.why: As graphics carried more visual information, music that stood out too much started to feel off; realistic graphics call for realistic ambience.
principles.how: Layer sounds like wind through leaves, feet on dirt and clinking armor, and mix each element to an appropriate level under the music.
principles.anti_pattern: Loud, foreground music fighting with detailed visuals.
principles.example: NES-style music played over modern games sounds noisy and off.
principles.quote: Realistic graphics, for example, call for realistic ambient sounds.

principles.principle: Make each song complement how the player is feeling
principles.why: The right approach depends on the game type, but music works best when it supports the player's emotional state.
principles.how: For each scene, note what the player should feel there and check that its music reinforces that feeling.
principles.quote: In any case, I'd say it's best to make songs that complement how the player is feeling.

summary: To be a director, develop a keen, personal way of seeing details and perspectives others miss, and pair it with good balance and clear communication, because that unique touch is what sets a game apart.
takeaways: Skilled directors share little except seeing things differently
Notice tiny details others miss in visuals, essence, animation, story
Balance quirkiness with good sense and clear communication
Use your own feelings to set your game apart

principles.principle: Train yourself to notice details and perspectives others miss
principles.why: The one trait good directors share is a keen sensibility that latches onto tiny details and sees things differently from other people.
principles.how: When reviewing builds or other games, write down the small details in visuals, game essence, animation and story that most people would overlook.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming there is one standard way to be a director.
principles.quote: If you show them something, or run an idea by them, they're the kind of people who'll latch onto tiny details, and perceive things that most others would miss.

principles.principle: Turn your personal thoughts and feelings into what distinguishes your game
principles.why: Directors use their own thoughts and feelings to set their games apart; the role, like a game, needs a touch only that person can give.
principles.how: For each major decision, state your personal take and how it differs from the genre's default, and keep it deliberately.
principles.quote: A director position—just like a game itself— calls for a personal, unique touch that only that person is capable of offering.

principles.principle: Pair a unique vision with balance and clear communication
principles.why: Quirkiness helps, but directors also need a good sense of balance and the skill to communicate their creative ideas; he can hardly think of directors who can't converse.
principles.how: Practice explaining your ideas to teammates until they can restate them accurately.
principles.anti_pattern: Being so idiosyncratic that the team can't follow your ideas.
principles.quote: They should probably be skilled at communicating their creative ideas, too.

summary: You can take enemies out of a game, but not the stress they provide: build every loop as stress → relief → growth → progress, and if there is no combat, find another source of stress.
takeaways: Fun comes from stress, then relief, growth and progress
You can remove enemies but must keep the stress they provide
Stress can come from peril, puzzles or prices, not only combat
Give collected resources something worth spending them on

principles.principle: Build every loop as stress, relief, growth, then progress
principles.why: Relief, growth and progress are what make a game fun, but they are hard to establish without initial stress from an obstacle.
principles.how: Map your core loop into the four steps and name what supplies each; add an obstacle, reward or next goal wherever a step is missing.
principles.anti_pattern: Removing obstacles entirely, which removes the relief and growth too.
principles.quote: Stress, relief, growth, and progress.

principles.principle: Replace removed enemies with another source of stress
principles.why: Enemies exist to provide stress and relief; a game without enemies still needs that stress, and extra stress relieved feels extra rewarding.
principles.how: If combat is cut, create stress through characters in peril, indirect obstacles or costs, and reward harder solutions with bigger progress.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming a no-combat game can work without stress.
principles.example: Undertale's Pacifist route overcomes enemies indirectly, which may be even more stressful and rewarding.
principles.quote: To summarize, it's possible to take enemies out of games if you want, but you still need the stress and relief they provide.

principles.principle: Give every saved-up resource a worthwhile use
principles.why: Paying for things is its own stress and relief: an expensive item lets players save up and look forward to owning it.
principles.how: Pair each resource with things to buy, including at least one expensive goal worth saving toward.
principles.anti_pattern: Infinite resources with no way to use them.
principles.example: A mining game with infinite resources and nothing to use them on would be pointless.
principles.quote: There'd be no point in a mining game where you can get infinite resources but have no way to use them, right?

summary: Every new work competes with all past works for people's time, so offer something fresh that can't be found anywhere else, and keep that broad view of the competition.
takeaways: New titles compete with every past title for players' time
Streaming makes film's competition with the back catalog fierce
Games are partly shielded by advancing technology and changing scale
Stand out by offering something fresh found nowhere else

principles.principle: Offer something fresh that players can't find elsewhere
principles.why: Markets are crowded because many creators keep entering them, so standing out requires something that can't be found in other works.
principles.how: In your pitch, state what your game offers that no existing game or other medium does, and protect that during development.
principles.quote: If you really want to stand out from the crowd, you need to offer something fresh that can't be found elsewhere.

principles.principle: Count past titles as competition for your players' time
principles.why: For the audience, time spent on something old is worth the same as time spent on something new, so the whole back catalog is competition.
principles.how: When positioning a game, list the older games, ports and other media competing for the same player's time, not just this year's releases.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming your only competition is other new releases.
principles.example: Subscription video services pit new films against decades of past titles.
principles.quote: From the viewer's perspective, the time spent watching something new is of equal value to time spent watching something old.

summary: Cut every second players spend not playing (waits, empty stretches, bloated cutscenes), because slowness is the one trap that can make nobody love your game.
takeaways: Slowness is the one trap that can make nobody love a game
Minimize time players spend not actually playing
Keep cutscenes lean; use them only as palate cleansers
Unavoidable waits must never feel like a development mistake

principles.principle: Measure and maximize the time the player is in control
principles.why: Games are full of fun experiences and making players wait to reach them is really bad; every second without fun is something to feel bad about.
principles.how: Time a session and split it into in-control, not-in-control and empty time, then set targets to shrink the last two.
principles.anti_pattern: Long stretches with nothing to do.
principles.quote: When I'm making a game, I pay attention to actual playtime— the amount of time the player has control.

principles.principle: Trim cutscenes that are needless downtime
principles.why: Cutscenes can serve as a palate cleanser, which beats keeping players busy constantly, but leaner cutscenes fit modern games better.
principles.how: Review each cutscene: keep those that give a deliberate breather and shorten or cut those that only delay play.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying on slowness to build suspense, which may not land today.
principles.quote: Leaner cutscenes tend to be a better fit for games nowadays.

principles.principle: Never let an unavoidable wait feel like a development mistake
principles.why: Some load times can't be optimized away, but a wait that feels like someone dropped the ball is what irritates players.
principles.how: Optimize loads as far as possible and make any remaining waits look deliberate rather than like an oversight.
principles.anti_pattern: Waits that look like bugs or forgotten slowdowns.
principles.quote: If that wait time feels like a mistake— like you're sitting around because someone dropped the ball in development— that's just irritating.

summary: You can invent a fresh concept even in a genre you're bad at: identify its game essence (risk and reward), change the core action rather than just its wording, and make each stage or character change the actual rules.
takeaways: Derive concepts from a genre's risk and reward, not your skill
Change the core action, not just its wording
Make each planet change rules, physics and audio, not just art
Late processing-speed changes broke his balance and raised difficulty

principles.principle: Design from the genre's risk and reward, even if you're bad at it
principles.why: He is bad at falling-block puzzles but could still propose Meteos by working out the principles of their game essence: stacking blocks is risk that careful play turns into a big reward.
principles.how: Write your genre's risk and reward in one sentence, then brainstorm other ways to discharge that risk than the default action.
principles.example: Meteos: matched blocks blast off into the air instead of disappearing.
principles.quote: Even though I'm not great at these games, I knew I could come up with a proposal if I just figured out the principles behind their game essence.

principles.principle: Change the core concept, not just the name of the action
principles.why: Bombs that destroy everything already existed, and calling clears 'vaporized' or 'demolished' wouldn't make the game new.
principles.how: Check whether a new idea changes what the player actually does; if it only renames the genre's verb, keep iterating.
principles.anti_pattern: Cosmetic novelty that reuses the standard clear action.
principles.example: Meteos's launch mechanic enabled secondary ignitions and air docking.
principles.quote: Whether blocks were "vaporized" or "demolished"— the wording itself wasn't the issue. I had to change the core concept.

principles.principle: Make each stage or character change the rules, not just the visuals
principles.why: In most puzzle games character choice barely changes play, while Meteos planets differ in block shapes, field width, launch behavior and audio, so controls feel different and players pick favorites.
principles.how: Give each stage or character distinct parameters such as field size, gravity, speed and piece types, plus its own music and sound effects.
principles.anti_pattern: Character select that only swaps art or slightly alters skills.
principles.example: Meteos planets: Boggob gains height each jump, Hevendor blocks vanish on match, Brabbit moves very slowly.
principles.quote: The controls feel drastically different when you switch planets, so I'm sure players had their favorites.

principles.principle: Lock processing speed before final balance tuning
principles.why: He tuned every planet himself, but processing speeds changed late in development and the game ended up harder than intended.
principles.how: Freeze frame timing and processing speed before final tuning, and redo balance passes after any late performance change.
principles.anti_pattern: Changing processing speed after balance has been tuned.
principles.example: Meteos released more difficult than he intended.
principles.quote: I personally tuned the balance for each individual planet, but we changed processing speeds late in dev, resulting in a game that was more difficult than I intended.

summary: As soon as the bones of your game exist, design its rewards, and make sure every saved-up reward has something appealing to spend it on, because rewards are where player investment comes from.
takeaways: Rewards are the main source of player investment
Design rewards right after the game's bones exist
Pair every currency with appealing, suitable things to buy
Crafted results must feel like profit and a must-have
Don't let collecting become the only activity

principles.principle: Design the reward system as soon as the core game works
principles.why: Progress alone doesn't motivate players in modern games; rewards are the source of their investment.
principles.how: Once the bones are in place, list what every enemy, mission and activity grants and where each reward is used.
principles.quote: Rewards are key to keeping players engaged! So like I said earlier, you should make them the first thing you consider.

principles.principle: Pair every accumulated currency with appealing things to spend it on
principles.why: Money or points saved over time need a spending outlet, and if what you can buy is unappealing or unsuitable it won't turn out well.
principles.how: Design the spending side alongside the earning side and check each purchasable item is desirable and fits the game.
principles.anti_pattern: Currencies with dull or ill-fitting sinks.
principles.quote: Money or points—numerical rewards you save up over time— should naturally come packaged with a way to spend them.

principles.principle: Make crafted items feel like profit and a must-have
principles.why: Turning collected materials into something new is particularly effective, but only if players feel they profit and want the result.
principles.how: Price recipes so the output is clearly worth more than its materials, and make outputs things players actively want.
principles.anti_pattern: Loops where gathering materials is the only thing you do.
principles.quote: It's vital the player feels like they're profiting, and that the end product is a must-have.

principles.principle: Grant collectibles as rewards instead of unlocking them at start
principles.why: A collection feature has no joy if everything is available from the beginning.
principles.how: Gate characters, equipment and collection items behind play so each one is earned.
principles.anti_pattern: Unlocking everything from the start.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Spirits would have no joy if unlocked at the start.
principles.quote: In Smash Bros. Ultimate, for example, if we didn't grant Spirits as rewards but had them unlocked at the start, there'd be no joy in the feature.

summary: Train yourself to feel frame durations (at 60 fps) by counting "1-and-2-and," so you can specify timing, speed and distance in frames and catch mistakes when the build doesn't match.
takeaways: Frames measure time, so they underlie all speed and distance
Count "1-and-2-and": each beat is about 30 frames
Half a beat is about 15 frames, like a Smash Attack
Estimate other durations relative to memorized reference points
A trained sense catches code or data timing errors

principles.principle: Learn to feel frames by counting "1-and-2-and" at 60 fps
principles.why: Frames are the basis for all movement in games; with no stopwatch for frames, you need a trained sense to ballpark them.
principles.how: Clap seconds saying "1-and-2-and-3-and": each beat is about 30 frames and half a beat about 15; check against an engine frame counter.
principles.quote: Frames are the basis for all movement in games. That's why it's so important to learn how long they are.

principles.principle: Estimate frame counts relative to memorized reference moves
principles.why: Approximating from known anchors is how to judge durations like 20 frames, which sits a little past halfway between 0 and 30.
principles.how: Memorize reference timings from familiar games and estimate new values by their distance from the 0/15/30-frame anchors.
principles.example: 15 frames is about a Smash Attack's input-to-release in Smash Bros. and a standard kick's startup in Tekken.
principles.quote: We approximate based on how far we are from these reference points.

principles.principle: Specify timing in frames and verify the build by feel
principles.why: Directors briefing the team with precise frame assignments must be able to count frames, and even correct specs can be broken by code or data errors.
principles.how: Write exact frame numbers into move and animation specs, then play each move and investigate when it feels off.
principles.anti_pattern: Assigning frame counts you can't actually feel.
principles.quote: Even once you successfully implement the right frame counts, you may sometimes still end up with errors in the code or data.

summary: The recovery after an attack takes up most of its screen time, so animate it big and expressive to sell the attack's weight, and place cancel frames where players expect to get control back.
takeaways: Follow-through (recovery) occupies the most screen time of an attack
Hits register a quarter to a third into the move
Strong attacks need proportionally long vulnerability for push and pull
Don't interpolate straight to standby; keep motion big and weighty
Place cancel frames where players expect to regain control

principles.principle: Give strong attacks proportionally long recovery
principles.why: Lead-ins should be fast for responsiveness, but without vulnerability matching an attack's strength there is no push and pull and the game feels unrefined.
principles.how: Have hits register about 1/4 to 1/3 into the move (1/5 for fast ones), keep moves under one second, and lengthen recovery as power rises.
principles.anti_pattern: Powerful attacks with little vulnerability afterward.
principles.example: Even Smash Bros. Smash Attacks with large vulnerability windows almost never exceed one second.
principles.quote: But assuming you want push and pull, strong attacks should leave a character proportionally vulnerable afterward, or the game will feel really unrefined.

principles.principle: Animate recovery as a big, weighty motion, not a blend to idle
principles.why: The hit itself ends in a fraction of a second, so the follow-through is what shows players what the character just did and how heavy it was.
principles.how: Keep the motion going as long as possible with large movements that carry the strike's momentum before returning to standby.
principles.anti_pattern: Interpolating straight from the hit back to the standby pose.
principles.quote: The follow-through after an attack determines the impact of the attack itself. Don't let it fizzle out—keep those actions expressive right to the end.

principles.principle: Place cancel frames where players expect to regain control
principles.why: Cancel frames let the player act early during the return to standby, and their timing must match when people expect control back.
principles.how: Mark a cancel window in the latter part of each recovery and playtest whether it lines up with players' instinctive timing.
principles.example: Smash Bros. attack breakdowns mark where cancel frames end recovery.
principles.quote: The timing of these cancel frames should fit with when people might expect they'll have control back.

summary: If you can't hide load times in immersive presentation, clearly show a simple, elegant loading indicator that fits your game's world, and don't build presentation around development-build load times that will change.
takeaways: Hide loads in presentation only if done seamlessly
Otherwise clearly indicate that the game is loading
Load times change before release; don't build presentation around them
Make indicators simple, elegant and evocative of the game world

principles.principle: Clearly show loading when you can't hide it in presentation
principles.why: Today's players have little interest in waiting, and a wait is easier to accept when the game indicates it is loading.
principles.how: If a load can't be woven into an immersive transition, display a loading indicator right away.
principles.anti_pattern: Silent waits with no indication.
principles.quote: if you're unable to pull that off, I'd say you're better served just clearly stating that the game is loading.

principles.principle: Don't tie presentation length to development-build load times
principles.why: Load times usually get optimized and shortened between development and release.
principles.how: Use a reusable indicator that can appear for any duration, and only use load-masking transitions that still work if final loads are shorter.
principles.anti_pattern: Transitions timed to today's slow dev loads.
principles.example: The first Resident Evil's door animation hid loading so well that an icon would ruin the illusion.
principles.quote: And so, you may not always want to make loading screens depend on presentation.

principles.principle: Make loading indicators simple, elegant and true to your world
principles.why: Indicators should be ready to display whenever needed, and plain "Now Loading..." text is rare these days.
principles.how: Design one minimal animated indicator styled after your game's world and use it everywhere.
principles.anti_pattern: Generic "Now Loading..." text.
principles.quote: If you're going to use indicators, try to make them evoke the atmosphere of your game's world!

summary: Effects pack a lot of information into an instant, so study them in slow motion to learn how they're built, and fill your game with plenty of exciting effects, because without them it looks plain.
takeaways: Effects pack much information into an instant
Study effects in slow motion with backgrounds disabled
Careful observation is a shortcut to success
Removing effects makes a game look plain

principles.principle: Study effects in slow motion with backgrounds disabled
principles.why: Visual effects deliver a great deal of information in an instant, so they are hard to parse at full speed, and careful observation is a shortcut to success.
principles.how: Record effects with slow motion on and backgrounds off, then step through them frame by frame to learn their shapes, timing and layering.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate effects recorded in slow motion with backgrounds disabled.
principles.quote: Careful observation is a shortcut to success no matter what you're making, so I hope this proves to be a valuable resource.

principles.principle: Fill your game with plenty of exciting effects
principles.why: Effects fly by too quickly to notice, but without them the game looks plain, and different effects make the same game feel quite different.
principles.how: Compare key scenes with effects on and off; if the difference is small, add more and bolder effects.
principles.anti_pattern: Skimping on effects because they are on screen only briefly.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate with effects removed looks pretty plain.
principles.quote: The same game can end up feeling quite different with different effects, so if you really want to bring your game to life, fill it with plenty of exciting effects!

summary: Development and marketing multiply each other, and an unknown game may as well not exist, so even as a developer, plan from the start how your work will help make the game known.
takeaways: An unknown game may as well not exist
Development and marketing are multiplicative
Make in-game assets usable for marketing too
Developers should review updates and suggest marketing ideas

principles.principle: Treat making the game known as important as making it good
principles.why: Development and marketing spin on the same axle; the success of one is proportional to the other, and with 10,000+ Steam releases in 2021 nobody finds games by chance.
principles.how: From early in development, plan what the dev team will contribute to promotion, such as reveal trailers or an official info site.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming a good game will be discovered on its own.
principles.example: Smash Bros. fighter reveal movies and the Smash Bros. Dojo site.
principles.quote: An unknown game may as well not exist.

principles.principle: Create in-game assets so they can double as marketing material
principles.why: He always considers that assets like fighter artwork may be used outside the game as well.
principles.how: Produce key art, renders and cinematics at a quality and format that marketing can reuse.
principles.example: Smash Bros. fighter artwork.
principles.quote: When creating assets like fighter artwork needed for the game itself, I always consider that it may be used elsewhere outside the game as well.

principles.principle: Get the marketing plan and review official updates before posting
principles.why: He asks publishers for marketing and operations details so he can suggest ideas, and checks every official social and website update.
principles.how: Request the marketing and operations schedule and set up a review step for official posts.
principles.anti_pattern: Flooding your personal account with announcements, which can rub people the wrong way.
principles.quote: I don't personally write the updates that appear on the game's official Twitter account or the website, but I always check them over and offer feedback.

summary: Protect your eyes for a long career. Brightness, glasses and eyedrops help, but nothing works as well as changing your work environment, for example moving your monitor farther away.
takeaways: Handheld and close screens strain his eyes; he plays in TV mode
Under 60 cm from the monitor tired his eyes fast
He now keeps at least one meter, with a bigger monitor
Changing the work environment beats glasses, eyedrops or supplements

principles.principle: Fix your work environment first to reduce eye strain
principles.why: Brightness, blue-light glasses, eyedrops and supplements help, but nothing is as effective as changing the work environment.
principles.how: If your monitor is under 60 cm away, move it back toward at least one meter and use a larger monitor to compensate.
principles.anti_pattern: Long sessions with screens close to your eyes.
principles.example: He had severe eye strain and dry eyes during Smash Bros. Ultimate's development.
principles.quote: There are plenty of methods out there, but I'd say nothing is as effective as changing your work environment.

principles.principle: Match screen brightness to your surroundings
principles.why: Lowering brightness to match the room is one of several ways to reduce eye strain.
principles.how: Adjust monitor brightness to the room's lighting, and add glasses or eyedrops as secondary measures.
principles.quote: You can lower screen brightness to better match your surroundings.

summary: A competitive game needs enough mechanics to create push and pull that lasts hundreds of matches, but every rule must earn its place, so question your genre's "givens" at the start of each project.
takeaways: A one-punch fighter has no push and pull
Each added mechanic, like a punishable kick, builds depth
Games meant for hundreds of matches need some complexity
Cut rules that don't add push and pull
Re-examine your genre's givens at every new project

principles.principle: Add mechanics one at a time, each creating new push and pull
principles.why: A fighter with one punch and no walking has no push and pull; walking adds range, and jumping, guarding and throwing each add depth.
principles.how: Start from a minimal core and add one mechanic at a time, writing down the new decision it creates; cut any that create none.
principles.anti_pattern: Rules that add complexity without push and pull.
principles.example: Street Fighter II's moves each had specific roles, giving incredible depth.
principles.quote: Each of these features gradually brings depth to our game.

principles.principle: Give stronger moves longer recovery so whiffs can be punished
principles.why: Making the kick recover longer than the punch means a miss can be countered, which is the point where push and pull appears.
principles.how: Pair each move's power with matching recovery so committing to a strong move carries risk.
principles.quote: If we give the kick a longer recovery than the punch so it can be countered if you miss. Well, now we've got some push and pull.

principles.principle: Re-examine inherited genre rules at the start of every project
principles.why: Genres with a long history accumulate complicated rules that don't add push and pull, and creators take familiar features for granted.
principles.how: At kickoff, list conventions inherited from the genre or your last game and decide whether each still earns its place.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating genre conventions as fixed givens.
principles.example: Every Super Smash Bros. has slightly different jump mechanics because he re-examines them.
principles.quote: To some extent, there's no avoiding complexity in games— but it's best to always approach your "givens" as if they aren't givens at all.

principles.principle: Size a game's depth to how many matches it must sustain
principles.why: Casual fun has its place, but a game meant to last hundreds of matches needs a certain level of complexity, and moves too hard to perform hide the push and pull.
principles.how: Decide the target lifespan first, then add depth to match while keeping inputs easy enough to feel the push and pull.
principles.anti_pattern: Inputs so hard players can't feel the push and pull.
principles.example: The original Street Fighter (1987) had many moves that were too hard to pull off.
principles.quote: Still, if you want your game to last through hundreds upon hundreds of matches, its mechanics will need to deliver a certain level of complexity.

summary: When you can't get started, stop thinking and start the task right now. Motivation follows action, and success comes from steady output.
takeaways: When stuck, start the task immediately
Motivation comes after you begin, not before
Cut off social media, videos and games while working
Success requires steady output

principles.principle: Start the task now instead of waiting for motivation
principles.why: There's no point in overthinking when unmotivated; motivation comes later, once your hands are moving.
principles.how: Take the first physical step at once: open the document and write a line, or open the canvas and draw.
principles.anti_pattern: Waiting to feel motivated before starting.
principles.quote: If you're feeling unmotivated, there's no point in overthinking it. The time is now. Get those hands moving.

principles.principle: Cut off distractions and keep a steady output
principles.why: Social media, video sites, the internet and games are tempting, and you won't succeed without steady output.
principles.how: Close distracting apps before each work block and produce something every day; save planning tricks for after you've started.
principles.anti_pattern: Overthinking what the work means before doing it.
principles.quote: You won't succeed without steady output.

summary: State every speed in an explicit unit the whole team shares (pixels per frame for sprites, real-world or distance-per-frame units for 3D), and train your sense of speed so your parameters land close the first time.
takeaways: Speed equals distance divided by time
Sprite games used pixels per frame; canvas sizes differ by hardware
Real-scale 3D lets you use real units like km/h
Character size changes how fast a speed feels
Specify units so the whole team shares them

principles.principle: Specify a unit for every speed in specs and parameters
principles.why: You can't get far in specs or parameters if you can't convey speed, so the whole team must share units of measurement.
principles.how: Choose a project unit (px/frame for sprites, km/h or m/frame for real-scale 3D), document it and include it in every parameter name.
principles.anti_pattern: Unitless speed values, or reusing values across hardware with different pixel counts.
principles.example: NES, Game Boy and Super NES canvases differed, so equal speed values gave different results.
principles.quote: So, it's essential you get your whole team on the same page when it comes to distances by specifying your units of measurement.

principles.principle: Build to real-world scale to use real speeds as-is
principles.why: When characters and environments are defined in real units, real-life speeds can be used directly, which is much easier to understand.
principles.how: Model characters and environments at real scale; switch to distance per frame where the game needs it.
principles.quote: As long as characters and environments were defined in real-life units of measurement, we could use real speeds as-is in the game.

principles.principle: Judge speed relative to the character's size
principles.why: A speed that sounds slow in km/h is fast for a tiny character.
principles.how: When tuning, compare speed to the character's own body size, not just the raw number.
principles.example: Kirby Air Ride used km/h, and low-looking speeds were fast because Kirby is only a 20 cm square.
principles.quote: These speeds might seem to be rather low, but that's because Kirby is only as big as a 20cm square.

principles.principle: Stylize locomotion when speed outruns a natural walk cycle
principles.why: Pit moved so fast that normally animated legs could never keep up.
principles.how: For very fast movement, use bounding or sliding motions instead of a sped-up realistic leg cycle.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising gave Pit a bounding motion and let him slide along the ground.
principles.quote: If we animated him normally, his legs would never keep up— so we instead gave him more of a bounding motion, and let him slide along the ground.

summary: Teach controls through real challenges woven into the game's progression, not through separate practice stages, so the tutorial never feels like work or slows down the start.
takeaways: Teach through real challenges, not dummy practice stages
Getting straight into the game keeps players engaged
Button prompts must cover every remappable button
Confine players to small areas to teach movement skills
Weave tutorials into progression so they never feel like work

principles.principle: Teach controls through real challenges, not dummy practice stages
principles.why: Players who get straight into the game and learn by overcoming real challenges are more engaged and excited.
principles.how: Replace separate training stages with early real obstacles that require the action being taught.
principles.anti_pattern: Forced practice stages against dummy opponents.
principles.example: Donkey Kong Country 3 spells out buttons with bananas in an early stage.
principles.quote: When introducing a game, it's better to give players real challenges to face, then let them learn by overcoming said challenges.

principles.principle: Teach movement skills in a small area that requires the skill to exit
principles.why: Many games confine players to a small area and make them use the new movement skill to progress, teaching it inside the game's flow.
principles.how: Build a compact enclosed space whose only exit needs the new skill, placed right after the player acquires it.
principles.quote: For movement-based skills, many games will confine players to a small area, then make them use the skill to progress.

principles.principle: Show button prompts that follow the player's remapping
principles.why: Visual control guides have to account for button remapping, so icons must exist for every button the player could use.
principles.how: Drive prompts from the live input mapping and create icons for every possible button.
principles.anti_pattern: Prompts hardcoded to default buttons.
principles.quote: When showing button icons, you need to cover every possible button the player can use.

principles.principle: Weave tutorials into progression so they never slow the opening
principles.why: Any method works if players learn the controls, but tutorials that feel like work or slow down the start hurt the game.
principles.how: Teach each mechanic at the point progression first needs it; weigh skill-preview modes against their labor and load times.
principles.anti_pattern: Skill-preview features whose load times deter players from using them.
principles.quote: Tutorials shouldn't feel like work, or like they're slowing down the beginning of the game— instead, try to weave them into the game's progression itself.

summary: Understand *why* a genre's core action is fun (its risk and reward) instead of copying the action itself. Then you can come up with ideas quickly, even in genres you're bad at.
takeaways: Jigsaws and Pentomino lack push and pull; Tetris has risk-reward
Stacking blocks is the risk; clearing lowers it
Big multi-clears require great risk, so they feel better
Speed-ups and post-landing moves raise risk and excitement
Ask why an action is fun, not which action

principles.principle: Design from why an action is fun, not from the action itself
principles.why: Understanding the genre's essence let him come up with Meteos's launching idea in five minutes despite being bad at the genre.
principles.how: Before fixing the core action, write why the genre's usual action is fun and brainstorm other actions that deliver the same payoff.
principles.anti_pattern: Starting from the assumption that blocks have to disappear.
principles.example: Meteos launches blocks instead of erasing them.
principles.quote: You shouldn't start your design with the idea that blocks have to disappear, but instead consider why it's fun to make those blocks disappear.

principles.principle: Make the biggest rewards require the biggest accumulated risk
principles.why: Taking great risk to clear many blocks at once makes the result feel even better.
principles.how: Tie your largest payoffs to states where the player has let danger build up.
principles.example: Tetris: stacking high is risky, and clearing lots of blocks at once needs that risk.
principles.quote: You need to put yourself at great risk in order to clear lots of blocks at once, which makes the end result feel even better.

principles.principle: Escalate risk over time to keep tension rising
principles.why: Tetrominos gradually falling faster raises risk and makes the game more exciting.
principles.how: Increase speed or pressure steadily over a session so decisions get harder as play goes on.
principles.example: Tetris pieces speed up as time passes.
principles.quote: The way Tetrominos gradually start falling quicker as time passes also serves to heighten risk, and thus makes the game more exciting.

principles.principle: Let skilled players cling to life at the edge
principles.why: Letting pieces be rotated and slid after landing lets players cling to life, which invites even greater risk-taking.
principles.how: Add last-moment recovery options so players can push their luck further.
principles.example: Later Tetris ports allowed rotating and sliding pieces after they land.
principles.quote: a significant addition, as being able to cling to life like this invites even greater risk.

summary: Finishing a game ("mastering up") often feels more bruising than triumphant, so thank the staff who got through it with you, and approach other people's games with gratitude for the same struggle.
takeaways: Mastering up often feels wounding rather than triumphant
Show appreciation to staff who endured the hardship
Online updates removed the clear end and closure
NES-era ROMs were hand-delivered by bullet train
Approach other developers' games with gratitude

principles.principle: Show appreciation to the staff when you master up
principles.why: Finishing usually involves tough decisions and cut content, so the moment can feel wounding, which makes you want to thank those who made it through.
principles.how: At master-up, explicitly recognize and thank the team, whatever state the project ended in.
principles.quote: Still, it makes you want to show appreciation for the staff that made it through that hardship with you.

principles.principle: Plan for post-release fixes; master-up may not be the end
principles.why: With online updates you may keep chipping away at issues that slipped into the final version, so there is no clean end.
principles.how: Reserve people and time after master-up for patching issues in the shipped version.
principles.quote: And if you can do online updates, you might have to keep chipping away at issues that slipped into the final version.

principles.principle: Approach other developers' games with gratitude
principles.why: Many other developers go through the same struggles to finish their games.
principles.how: When playing or critiquing others' games, keep in mind the cuts and hardships behind them.
principles.quote: I know that pain all too well, so I try to approach the games I play with gratitude.

summary: Budget for management overhead (ten people generally produce about seven people's worth of work), and keep a growing team aligned with regular meetings where each subteam shows what it has finished.
takeaways: Ten people generally produce about seven people's work
Teams need workload managers, communicators and creative supervisors
Promoting a skilled creator to lead costs their output
Bigger teams take longer to align on tools, security, rules
Hold meetings where subteams present their finished work

principles.principle: Budget for management: ten people yield about seven people's work
principles.why: Running a team takes management time: workloads, outside communication and creative supervision all pull people away from production.
principles.how: Plan schedules assuming roughly 70% effective output from headcount, with more overhead as the team grows, and name who owns each management role.
principles.anti_pattern: Planning as if headcount equals output.
principles.quote: It depends on the situation, of course, but 10 people can generally produce seven people's worth of work.

principles.principle: Expect to lose a skilled creator's output when they lead
principles.why: Skilled workers moving into leadership can't replicate their output at scale; they become the brains who set direction and maintain quality.
principles.how: When promoting a strong creator to lead, backfill their production work in the schedule.
principles.anti_pattern: Expecting new leads to keep their full individual output.
principles.quote: When an experienced creative eye shifts over to the management side, that obviously means you lose the share of work they would have produced.

principles.principle: Hold regular meetings where each subteam presents its finished work
principles.why: It lets everyone see the whole project, builds presentation skills and deepens awareness that they are making something for others.
principles.how: Schedule a recurring showcase where each subteam, such as the character team, presents what it finished that period.
principles.quote: To help team members get a top-down view of the whole project, I recommend holding meetings where each subteam presents the fruits of their labor.

summary: Choose deliberately between exaggerated and realistic sound. Exaggeration sells impact in games like fighters, which are nothing like real fighting, while realistic sounds can supply information that simple graphics can't.
takeaways: Realistic fighting sounds would just be weak slaps
Fighting games are nothing like real fighting; exaggerate
Realistic visuals make exaggerated sounds feel stranger
Realistic sounds can fill information gaps in simple graphics
Balance exaggerated and realistic sound for a substantial world

principles.principle: Exaggerate impact sounds instead of using realistic ones
principles.why: Real punches would sound like a bunch of slaps, and forgetting that fighting games aren't real fighting pulls you away from the essence you want.
principles.how: Design combat hits as exaggerated sounds and compare them against realistic recordings to confirm they carry more weight.
principles.anti_pattern: Literal realism in combat audio.
principles.example: Street Fighter II's impact sounds are incredibly fake but effective.
principles.quote: If you don't remember right from the start that fighting games are nothing like actual fighting, you'll end up drifting far away from the game essence you want.

principles.principle: Use realistic material sounds to fill in what simple graphics can't show
principles.why: Lifelike sounds help players fill in missing information, giving meaning and weight to otherwise simple visuals.
principles.how: Give each material and action its own realistic sound, such as different sounds for placing wood and stone.
principles.example: Minecraft's building sounds let you feel the weight of wood and stone despite cube graphics.
principles.quote: The relatively lifelike sound effects help people to fill in the gaps in information.

principles.principle: Balance sound exaggeration against how realistic the visuals are
principles.why: The more realistic the visuals, the stranger exaggerated sounds feel, and the right balance makes the world feel more substantial.
principles.how: Decide per sound category whether its job is impact or information, and tune exaggeration to the game's visual realism.
principles.quote: Sound effects can be either exaggerated or realistic. By finding the right balance in your game, you can really help make its world feel more substantial.

summary: When supervising art, show rather than tell: a 5–10 minute retouch of the artist's own piece gets the direction across better than words, and then the artist does the real work of finishing it.
takeaways: Show art direction instead of describing it in words
A 5-10 minute retouch beats a verbal explanation
Boost contrast and hue-shift light to enrich flat backgrounds
Keep glowing elements like magma easy on the eyes
Retouches chart the course; artists do the real work

principles.principle: Give art feedback with a quick retouch instead of words
principles.why: Palette and contrast changes are hard to explain verbally, and a retouch taking about five to ten minutes is more efficient than explaining.
principles.how: Spend 5-10 minutes on a rough paintover of the artist's piece and send it side by side with the original.
principles.anti_pattern: Trying to retouch every asset, or long verbal descriptions of visual changes.
principles.example: Retouched backgrounds for a Spirits exploration cave, the Marx boss fight and a World of Light path.
principles.quote: When supervising a game's graphics, there's no better way to explain what you want than by just showing it.

principles.principle: Enrich flat backgrounds with contrast and hue-shifted light
principles.why: Introducing a complex color mesh to a monochromatic background improved the piece as a whole.
principles.how: Duplicate the layer, boost contrast, shift the hue, erase the shifted layer where light would hit, then harmonize the colors.
principles.anti_pattern: Understated, monochrome palettes.
principles.example: His Photoshop retouch of the Spirits cave gave the purple layer a reflective glow.
principles.quote: By introducing a complex color mesh to the monochromatic background, we improved the piece as a whole

principles.principle: Keep bright glowing elements from straining the eyes
principles.why: He wanted more contrast and heat on a World of Light pathway but avoided making the magma too bright so it wouldn't be hard on the eyes.
principles.how: Raise contrast to sell heat while capping the brightness of large glowing areas.
principles.anti_pattern: Overly bright magma or glow.
principles.example: World of Light pathway magma.
principles.quote: I avoided making the magma too bright so it wouldn't be hard on the eyes.

principles.principle: Treat retouches as direction and let artists execute
principles.why: Supervision is charting the creative course; reaching release quality takes serious work by the artist, and first-try approvals are best for everyone.
principles.how: Label retouches as examples and leave final execution to the artist.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating the director's retouch as final art.
principles.quote: In the end, supervision is really just charting the creative course.

summary: Game characters lose much of the information real people convey, so exaggerate performances and animations ("too much" is "just right"), especially when characters are small on screen.
takeaways: Polygon characters lose information real humans convey
Make up for it with big performances: too much is just right
Raw motion capture rarely works as-is
Small or distant characters need even bigger motion

principles.principle: Exaggerate animations to make up for information game characters lack
principles.why: Game characters lose a wide range of the information real humans offer, and no part of them truly exists, so 'too much' is 'just right'.
principles.how: Push poses, arcs and accents beyond realistic levels in both cutscenes and gameplay, and make a sword swing more than just a swing.
principles.anti_pattern: Literal, realistic motions that come up short where it matters.
principles.example: Clock Tower 3's over-the-top cutscenes, directed by Kinji Fukasaku.
principles.quote: With polygon-based characters, you lose a wide range of information that real humans offer, so you have to make up for that with big performances.

principles.principle: Push motion capture bigger instead of using it raw
principles.why: Motion capture data generally can't be dropped straight into a game and work; going really big tends to look best.
principles.how: Treat capture as a starting point and exaggerate it before it ships.
principles.anti_pattern: Dropping mocap straight into the game.
principles.quote: When you're using motion capture to make animations, you generally can't drop that data straight into the game and have it work.

principles.principle: Scale exaggeration to the character's on-screen size
principles.why: Motion that works up close feels far too understated when the character is small or far away.
principles.how: Review animations at the real gameplay camera distance and size, and exaggerate further where they read as weak.
principles.anti_pattern: Judging animations only in close-up views.
principles.quote: Stay mindful of your character's screen presence, size, and controls, then go big to let those animations really pack a punch!

summary: When adapting an existing hit to a new format (here, a handheld digital pet), reuse its proven push and pull, smooth out growth-stage walls, add small touches that sell the fantasy, and test on the real production hardware before release.
takeaways: Reuse an existing hit's proven push and pull when adapting
Prevent weak growth stages from walling players in battle
Small touches like grazing sell the pet fantasy
Test timers on production hardware; hunger ran too fast
Small team, remote work and a wooden dev board

principles.principle: Test timing-based systems on the production hardware before release
principles.why: He never tested on the production handheld; likely due to a processing-speed difference, the Mushi gets hungry faster than planned and puts unintended stress on players.
principles.how: Before release, run hunger, fatigue and growth timers on the final hardware and compare their rates with the design values.
principles.anti_pattern: Shipping having tested only on a development board.
principles.example: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking's Mushi almost always wants food.
principles.quote: Before it was done, I never got the chance to test the game out on the production handheld. As a result, there's an issue in the final version.

principles.principle: Smooth growth-stage power dips so players don't hit a wall
principles.why: In pet games, growth stages are stronger or weaker than others, which can stall players in battle.
principles.how: Check each growth stage's battle strength and adjust opponents or stats so no stage becomes a wall.
principles.quote: In pet games, different growth stages will be stronger or weaker than others. So, we took care not to let players run into a wall in battles.

principles.principle: Sell a creature fantasy with small, believable behaviors
principles.why: Depicting the Mushi grazing on its meal instead of scarfing it instantly gave a stronger sense of raising a pet, and hidden behaviors add depth.
principles.how: Animate everyday actions over time and add hidden responses, like a pet adjusting its schedule to when it is woken.
principles.example: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking: grazing on food; waking it early shifts its schedule.
principles.quote: For example, instead of having it instantly scarf down food, we depicted it grazing on its meal to capture that "pet" feeling.

principles.principle: Carry a proven push-and-pull core into adaptations
principles.why: Mushiking's rock-paper-scissors battles, with each Mushi specializing in one shape, already created push and pull through reading the opponent.
principles.how: When adapting a hit to a new format, keep its tested core interaction and spend design effort on what the new format adds.
principles.example: Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking arcade battles via rock-paper-scissors.
principles.quote: Each Mushi specialized in one of the three shapes, which led to the game's push and pull.

summary: In text-heavy games, use text effects (size, color, animation, font) to convey emotion, and build them as editable script so translators can restyle the emphasis for each language.
takeaways: Text size, color, animation and font convey emotion
Make text effects editable script, not hardcoded
Let translators set emphasis natural to their language
Manga techniques pack lots of expression into little space

principles.principle: Use text effects to convey emotion in text-heavy games
principles.why: Changing how certain letters or words display conveys a character's emotions and adds flavor, making such effects almost essential.
principles.how: Support inline changes of size, color, animation and font on individual words in your dialogue system.
principles.anti_pattern: One flat text style throughout an expressive, text-heavy game.
principles.example: Japanese comics techniques like kakimoji and manpu.
principles.quote: But changing how certain letters or words are displayed can help better convey a character's emotions or add flavor to an otherwise straightforward presentation

principles.principle: Let translators edit text-effect scripting for each language
principles.why: Different languages have different styles of emphasis, so native speakers should decide what presentation reads naturally.
principles.how: Store effect tags in the localizable script so translators can add, move or remove emphasis without developer help.
principles.anti_pattern: Hardcoding text effects where only developers can change them.
principles.quote: It's best to let native speakers from each country consider natural presentation, which is exactly why you want to make it so that translators can edit the scripting themselves.

principles.principle: Pack expression into limited space with fonts, bubbles and symbols
principles.why: Comic techniques like varied fonts, speech-bubble types and symbols with clear meaning convey emotion concisely.
principles.how: Offer several speech-bubble styles and a few emotion symbols alongside text effects.
principles.example: Manpu such as a sweat bead or vein mark.
principles.quote: And with techniques like changing the font or varying the type of speech bubble, it's possible to pack lots of expression into a relatively limited space.
